SOURCE: "Node-as-Agent: Graph Agentic Network" (ReaGAN, Retrieval-augmented Graph Agentic Network), Minghao Guo, Xi Zhu, ... Yongfeng Zhang (Rutgers et al.). arXiv 2508.00429v5 [cs.CL], dated 21 Jul 2026. Preprint. The ACM template placeholder reads "Conference acronym 'XX, Woodstock, NY 2018", so no venue is confirmed. It is v5, and the reference list includes 2026 arXiv items.

COVERAGE: All 67,931 chars read, through the last appendix section (A.3). Nothing skipped. References were skimmed only for origins. Figure 4-7 bar values are not in the text layer, so I did not read them.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- ReaGAN is a frozen-LLM agentic node classifier that matches supervised GNNs only on Cora. It is below the best GNN on Citeseer and Chameleon.
  number: Cora 84.95±0.35 vs GCN 84.71, GraphSAGE 84.35. Citeseer 60.25±0.36 vs GraphSAGE 78.24, MLP-2 76.25, GCN 72.56. Chameleon 43.80±0.65 vs GPRGNN 67.48, GraphSAGE 62.15, GAT 42.93.
  setup: Node classification on text-attributed Cora, Citeseer and Chameleon. Split 60/20/20 train/val/test. Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct frozen via vLLM, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings. Baselines are PyG with "standard hyperparameters", trained on the same splits. Error bars come from an unstated number of runs. Baselines have no reported variance.
  quote: "ReaGAN (Ours)84.95±0.35 60.25±0.36 43.80±0.65" and "while some supervised methods like GraphSAGE and GPRGNN show higher accuracy, ReaGAN still maintains a strong competitive standing."
  where: Table 1, p7, Sec 3.1
  Caveat for the note: the abstract says "competitive". On Citeseer it is about 18 points below GraphSAGE and about 16 below MLP-2. The text calls 60.25 "comparable to several established GNNs", which is generous. GCN is low on Chameleon (28.18) and MixHop low everywhere, so the baselines are weakly tuned.
- Node-level design: each node is an agent with memory, planning, actions and a tool. Per layer, a frozen LLM reads the node's memory and picks LocalAggregation, GlobalAggregation, both, or NoOp. After L layers it predicts once.
  number: L typically 1-3; max reasoning layers 3.
  setup: Algorithm 1; Qwen2.5-14B.
  quote: "This process repeats for 𝐿 layers (typically 1–3), after which each node outputs a predicted label."
  where: Sec 2.8, Alg. 1
- Global aggregation is RAG over a structure-free node-text index with no edges, so semantically similar but structurally distant nodes can be retrieved.
  number: top-K = 5, up to 5 few-shot examples from local and 5 from global.
  setup: Cosine similarity over MiniLM embeddings. Prompt length 512 tokens. Label-diversity reranking and deduplication.
  quote: "•RAG Top-K: 5 •Max reasoning layers: 3 • Few-shot examples per node: up to 5 from local neighbors and 5 from global retrieval"
  where: A.3, Sec 2.4.2, 2.8
- Ablations: removing planning, local aggregation or global retrieval each lowers accuracy. Only qualitative: no numbers in text, bars in Fig 4.
  number: none
  setup: Cora, Citeseer, Chameleon, same model.
  quote: "Removing either component leads to a measurable degradation in accuracy"
  where: Sec 3.3, Fig 4
- Adaptive retrieval helps on sparse graphs. Strategy B (add global memory only when fewer than 2 local examples) beats always adding global (A) on Citeseer. Citeseer average degree is about 2.84, Cora's about 4.01.
  number: 2.84 vs 4.01; threshold <2 local entries.
  setup: Fig 5, three datasets. The mechanism is the authors' interpretation, not tested.
  quote: "Citeseer has an average node degree of approximately 2.84 (4, 732 edges/3, 327 nodes× 2), which is considerably lower than Cora's average degree of roughly 4.01"
  where: Sec 3.3, Table 2
- Showing label names hurts accuracy, so the final design anonymizes labels (Label_1 ...).
  number: none in text ("Sharp drop" annotation in Fig 6).
  setup: Cora and Citeseer only. Explanation (LLM semantic shortcut) is asserted, not tested.
  quote: "providing explicit, human-readable label names (e.g., "Machine Learning", "Databases") consistently degrades classification accuracy across all datasets."
  where: Sec 3.3 RQ4, Fig 6. Note that "all datasets" is stated but Fig 6 shows only Cora and Citeseer.
- With no graph evidence, the frozen LLM falls back on its priors.
  number: 45 fallback events on Cora: Theory 13, Probabilistic Methods 9, Neural Networks 8, Rule Learning 2.
  setup: Isolated nodes, sampled batch.
  quote: "Out of 45 recorded fallback mapping events on the Cora dataset, the agent favored "Theory" (13 times), "Probabilistic Methods" (9 times), and "Neural Networks" (8 times), while rarely guessing "Rule Learning" (2 times)."
  where: Sec 3.4
- A discrete action vocabulary with validation and fallback (invalid output becomes Prediction or NoOp) keeps the runtime from breaking. The LLM acts as a policy, and a deterministic layer mutates state.
  number: Fallback success rose from 0 of 27 to 33 of 33 (100%) between early and final versions. Different batches, "comparable", with no stated size or datasets.
  quote: "In a sampled batch, a fallback mechanism was triggered 27 times, yet 100% of these attempts failed to yield a valid state update" and "the execution success rate jumps to 100%"
  where: Sec 2.7, 3.4, Fig 7
- Cost: it is slower than a GNN or MLP forward pass.
  number: about 3.10 s per iteration per batch; 64 nodes in about 3 min 18 s.
  setup: 14B frozen LLM on A6000 GPUs via vLLM. "Scaling" is shown only at 20 and 64 nodes.
  quote: "Processing a batch of 64 nodes requires approximately 3 minutes and 18 seconds, yielding a consistent inference cost of roughly 3.10 seconds per iteration per batch."
  where: Sec 3.4
- Behaviour: early layers favour local aggregation, later layers more global (especially sparse nodes), predictions come late, and NoOp is rare. These are qualitative, with no counts.
  quote: "NoOp actions are relatively rare"
  where: Sec 3.2

LIMITS
- Authors concede: high latency and memory from multi-layer LLM calls. Only node classification on static text-attributed graphs. Needs more backbones, dynamic or heterogeneous graphs, link prediction and graph-level tasks. Performance depends on prompt construction, retrieved examples and memory selection.
- Not shown: any LLM other than Qwen2.5-14B (LLaMA and DeepSeek are named but not run). Comparison to other LLM-on-graph methods (PromptGFM, In-context RAG, which are only discussed) or to a non-agentic LLM+RAG few-shot baseline. The agentic gain is isolated only via No Planning, Local Only and Global Only. No numeric ablation values in text. Number of runs or seeds for ±. Contamination risk (Cora and Citeseer are in LLM pretraining) is not discussed. The "reasoning" mechanisms are asserted without probing. Baseline fairness: the supervised GNNs use the 60% train split while ReaGAN uses labeled examples as few-shot context, so "few-shot" is not matched. Chameleon, a heterophilous graph, is the weakest result.
- Dated: the Qwen2.5 and MiniLM stack. Table 2 lists Chameleon with 2,277 nodes and 5 classes.

BUILDS ON
- GCN (Kipf & Welling, [15]), GAT (Velickovic et al., ICLR 2018), GraphSAGE ([12]), APPNP ([16]), GPRGNN (Chien et al. 2020, arXiv), MixHop (Abu-El-Haija et al., ICML 2019), Revisiting heterophily (Luan et al., NeurIPS 2022, source of the MLP-2 baseline).
- CoGNN (Finkelshtein et al. 2023, arXiv), cooperative agents choosing broadcast or listen.
- Agent-based GNNs (Martinkus et al., ICLR 2023).
- Graph Agent Network (Liu et al. 2024, arXiv).
- LLM as GNN / PromptGFM (Zhu et al. 2024, arXiv).
- In-context graph learners (Li et al. 2024, arXiv).
- RAG (Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020).
- ReAct (Yao et al. 2022, printed as "Shinn Yao", arXiv).
- Reflexion (Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023).
- Memory Sharing for LLM agents (Gao & Zhang 2024).

CODE: Algorithm 1 (p3, layer-wise loop) is pseudocode only. The A.1 planning prompt requests JSON like {"action_type": "local aggregate" | "global aggregate" | "no_op"}, and the prediction prompt requests {"action_type": "predict", "predicted_label": "Label ID"}. No code release is mentioned.

FIGURES (candidate: one)
- Fig 2, p4: "Overview of ReaGAN." Four modules (Memory, Planning, Tools/RAG, Action) in a perceive, plan, act, update loop. It explains the architecture faster than prose.
- (Fig 1, p1 contrasts fixed message passing with per-node local/global/none, and is simpler if only the idea is needed.)

PROBLEMS
- Extraction of Figs 4-7 gives axis labels only, with no bar values.
- No embedded instructions found.
- The reference list has a duplicate entry ([19]/[20] Know the Ropes). Ref [33] cites DeepSeek-VL for "DeepSeek". Ref [43] is cited for Qwen, but the Qwen2.5 model used is not cited.
- The stray text in the extraction "A Technical Appendices..." is the real appendix.

TARGET NOTE: Use 13b-representation-learning-and-gnns.md (title "Embeddings and GNNs"). The paper is about replacing fixed GNN message passing with a per-node LLM planner, and Table 1 compares it with GCN, GAT and GraphSAGE. Note 13 ("Tasks and Features") is about task framing and features. 13b already lists arXiv sources, so this paper should go in its sources list. Frame it as a contrast to message passing, with the result mixed (wins on Cora only), not as a replacement for GNNs.
